unit.title: How agents work: the loop, tools and memory

lesson.title: Memory: the context window
lesson.subtitle: What an agent remembers, what it forgets, and how apps choose

video.title: Memory: the context window
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds, one recurring teacher character. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Okafor — science teacher, Nigeria (main character)
Mr Joseph Mwangi — computer studies teacher, Kenya (cameo)
Ms Amina Bello — primary teacher, Nigeria (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: A list: Today’s weather?!; I said tomorrow; Where did it go?.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: I told the agent which village, and it gave me today’s weather. I had asked about tomorrow, three messages earlier! It had simply forgotten. Where did my words go?

scenes.animation: The Darsi mark pops in; the title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: an agent’s memory, and why it forgets.

scenes.visual: A list: No memory of its own; Reads the whole text again; Its limit: the context window.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: A model has no memory of its own between turns. Each time, the app hands it the text so far, and it reads it all again. The most it can read at once is called its context window.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Darsi Tiny’s window holds three hundred and eighty-four tokens, about three or four requests. Big cloud models read about one hundred and twenty-eight thousand. Bigger windows forget less, but every request costs more time and money.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: When the text is longer than the window, something has to go. Whatever falls out, the model never sees again. It isn’t hidden somewhere: for the model, it’s gone.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: The app decides what stays. Keep everything, and the window fills: the fourth answer is cut off. Drop the oldest turns, and the start of a task can vanish. Or keep short notes: what was asked, and what was answered.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Quick check! The app drops the oldest turns. I said yes to the agent’s question, and it just greeted me. Why?

scenes.visual: A list: The question fell out; A lone “yes” = a greeting; The start of a task goes first.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: The question had fallen out. Without it, a lone yes means nothing, so Darsi Tiny treated it as a greeting. That’s the risk of dropping the oldest turns: the start of a task goes first.

scenes.visual: A list: Keep the question and the answer; Drop old calls and results; All 7 messages work.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Notes are the smart middle way. A finished request keeps only the question and the answer; its tool calls and results go. In the lab, with notes, all seven messages work in the same window.

scenes.visual: A list: Memory is about privacy too; What stays can be repeated; Keep pupils’ names and marks out; New task, new conversation.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Memory is also a privacy question. Whatever stays in the window, or in saved notes, the model can repeat. So keep pupils’ names and marks out, and start a new conversation for each task.

scenes.visual: A list: Keep everything; Drop the oldest; Keep notes; All seven work?.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: In the app, send the messages with Keep everything, and watch the window fill. Then try Drop the oldest at one hundred and twenty-eight tokens, and say yes. Last, keep notes, and see all seven work.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Your turn. A colleague pastes thirty pupils’ reports into one chat with a small agent, then asks about the first pupil. What might go wrong?

scenes.visual: Summary points: The window is its only memory; What falls out is gone; Notes keep what matters.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.on_screen_text: The window is its only memory · What falls out is gone · Notes keep what matters
scenes.narration: The first reports may have fallen out, so the answer could be made up. Remember: the window is the model’s only memory. What falls out is gone. And the app chooses what stays.

scenes.visual: A list: A story, one word each; Keep only the last ten words; Ask about the beginning; Who still remembers?.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: play the ten-word window. Tell a story on the board, one word each, but rub out all but the last ten words. Then ask about the beginning: who still remembers it?

checkpoints.prompt: The app drops the oldest turns. You say yes to the agent’s question, and it greets you. Why?

options.text: The question had fallen out of the window

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — the question had fallen out, so a lone yes meant nothing to it. Dropping the oldest turns loses the start of a task first.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — it never saw the question: it had fallen out of the window, so “yes” alone meant nothing.

checkpoints.prompt: A colleague pastes thirty pupils’ reports into one chat with a small agent, then asks about the first pupil. What might go wrong?

options.text: The first reports may have fallen out, so the answer could be made up
The agent will refuse to read reports

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — the first reports may no longer be in the window, and the model can’t know what it never saw. Pupils’ reports also don’t belong in a long chat without a school rule.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a small window can’t hold thirty reports. The first ones fall out, and the answer may be invented.
